title: Moving to university
description: Make your funding last, understand housing costs and navigate money away from home.

lessons.title: Make your money last the term
lessons.description: Turn a lump sum into a weekly plan.
reading_cards: Sam has £3,000 available for a 12-week term. After reserving £1,800 for rent and £240 for known travel costs, £960 remains: £80 a week for everything else. These are practice figures, not a recommended student budget.

A balance can look generous while already being committed. List payment dates and all living costs before deciding what is available for food, study materials and social spending. Keep a margin for costs you cannot predict.

Check your actual funding schedule and eligibility with your student finance body. Rules and payment patterns differ across the UK and by circumstances; a termly payment is an example, not a universal rule.
checklist: Write down the date and amount of your next confirmed funding payment.
Reserve money for rent and known costs before setting a weekly allowance.
Check whether your plan covers holidays as well as term time.

questions.prompt: Sam has £3,000 for 12 weeks, with £1,800 rent and £240 travel reserved. What is left per week?
questions.explanation: £3,000 − £1,800 − £240 = £960; £960 ÷ 12 = £80. Other expenses must still fit within it.

questions.prompt: Your account shows £900, but £650 rent is due before your next payment. What is a useful starting point?
options: Assume your next funding will arrive early
Reserve £650 and plan the remaining £250 around other costs
Treat the whole £900 as spending money
questions.explanation: Separate money already committed before deciding what you can spend.

questions.prompt: Your friend receives funding three times a year. What should you use for your own plan?
options: Their dates, because all UK funding is identical
The balance you hope to have
Your own award notice and payment dates
questions.explanation: Use confirmed details from your own funding provider, not another student’s schedule.

lessons.title: Look beyond the rent
lessons.description: Compare the total cost before committing.
reading_cards: A room advertised at £125 a week is not automatically cheaper than one at £145. Compare the number of weeks you must pay for, included bills, travel costs and money required before you move in.
For example, £125 for 51 weeks costs £6,375 in rent. £145 for 40 weeks costs £5,800. Check whether you also need somewhere to live outside the shorter contract.

Before signing or sending money, understand the agreement, deposit, guarantor requirements and who is responsible for payments. Housing rules vary by UK nation and type of accommodation. Ask the university housing team to explain unclear terms.
checklist: Compare rent over the full contract, not just one week.
List bills, upfront payments and travel separately.
Ask the university housing team to review terms you do not understand.

questions.prompt: Room A is £125 for 51 weeks; room B is £145 for 40 weeks. Ignoring other costs, which rent total is lower?
options: They cost the same
Room B: £5,800
Room A: £6,375
questions.explanation: Multiply the weekly price by the full contract length. A lower weekly price can mean a higher total.

questions.prompt: A listing says “bills included”. What is worth checking before signing?
options: Only the colour of the room
Nothing: every possible bill must be covered
Which bills, any usage caps and the full contract
questions.explanation: Clarify exactly what is included; do not assume a short advert contains all the terms.

questions.prompt: You do not understand a guarantor clause. What is the next step?
options: Ask for an explanation before agreeing
Sign now and read it later
Ask a friend to sign without explaining it
questions.explanation: A guarantor may take on financial responsibilities. Get the clause explained before anyone agrees.

lessons.title: Share a home, not confusion
lessons.description: Make a workable plan for household bills.
reading_cards: Four housemates estimate a shared bill at £120 a month and agree an equal split: £30 each. Decide who holds the account, when contributions arrive and how everyone can see the bill.
A private agreement about splitting costs does not replace the supplier or tenancy contract. Check who is legally responsible and plan what happens if someone leaves or cannot pay.

In Great Britain, households made up entirely of qualifying full-time students generally do not pay Council Tax; check the council’s evidence and application process. Mixed households need a separate check. Northern Ireland uses domestic rates instead, so do not assume the same exemption applies.
checklist: Agree contributions and payment dates with housemates.
Keep shared bills and payment records accessible to everyone involved.
Check Council Tax or domestic rates with the relevant authority for your home.

sources.title: GOV.UK · Full-time students and Council Tax

questions.prompt: A £120 monthly bill is shared equally between four people. What is each share?
questions.explanation: £120 divided by four is £30. Actual contributions depend on the agreement and bill.

questions.prompt: One housemate agrees to collect everyone’s share. What still needs checking?
options: Who is responsible under the supplier’s contract
Whether the private split cancels the contract
Whether nobody has to keep records
questions.explanation: An informal split does not automatically change liability to the supplier.

questions.prompt: A student moves to Northern Ireland. Should they assume the Great Britain Council Tax exemption applies?
options: Yes: showing a student card always cancels every bill
No: check domestic rates rules for that property
Yes: all UK property taxes have identical student rules
questions.explanation: Northern Ireland uses rates. Check the local rules rather than importing Council Tax assumptions.

lessons.title: When the plan does not stretch
lessons.description: Spot borrowing risks and ask for support early.
reading_cards: An overdraft is borrowing, even if an arranged student overdraft currently charges no interest. Check the limit, conditions and what changes when student status ends; it is not extra income.

If funding is delayed or essential costs do not fit, contact your university money or welfare team about available support. Help and eligibility vary. Avoid covering a continuing shortfall with repeated borrowing without advice.

Treat an unexpected funding message asking for a password or urgent payment with caution. Open your provider’s official site independently or contact them using a known number, rather than following the message link.
checklist: Find your university’s money advice or student support contact.
Read the terms of any overdraft you already use.
Check funding messages through a trusted channel.

questions.prompt: Your account includes a £500 arranged overdraft. How should you think about it?
options: Borrowing that needs repaying under its terms
An extra grant
Money that never needs repaying while you study
questions.explanation: An overdraft remains debt, including during an interest-free period.

questions.prompt: Your funding is late and rent is due. Which is a useful early step?
options: Take several loans before checking other options
Contact student support and the accommodation provider
Ignore all messages until funding arrives
questions.explanation: Explain the timing problem and ask what support or arrangements may be available.

questions.prompt: A text says your funding will be cancelled unless you enter your password through its link. What should you do?
options: Enter your password quickly
Forward the password to the sender instead
Check through the provider’s official site independently
questions.explanation: Use a trusted route to verify the claim. Urgency is not proof that a message is genuine.

lessons.title: Plan a food shop
lessons.description: Practise fitting a shopping list into a weekly amount.
reading_cards: Practice example: Alex has £35 for food this week. A planned shop costs £27, leaving £8. These are made-up figures, not a suggested food budget.
A short list can help you remember what you need. In this example, Alex checks the cupboard before buying another bag of rice.
A bigger packet does not always cost less per unit. Compare the price for the same amount, and consider whether you will use it all.
checklist: Try the example calculation with your own notes.

questions.prompt: Alex has £35 and spends £27. How much remains?
questions.explanation: £35 minus £27 leaves £8.

questions.prompt: What can Alex do before shopping?
options: Buy everything again
Check what is already in the cupboard
Ignore the shopping list
questions.explanation: Checking what is already there can prevent duplicate purchases.

questions.prompt: Which is cheaper per kilogram?
options: 500g for £2
1kg for £5
1kg for £3
questions.explanation: 500g for £2 is £4 per kilogram. £3 per kilogram is the lowest of these example prices.

lessons.title: Split shared costs clearly
lessons.description: Practise dividing a bill with housemates.
reading_cards: Practice example: three housemates agree to split a £60 shared purchase equally. Each person contributes £20.
Before buying something together, agree what is shared, the amount and who will pay. A simple written note can help everyone remember the agreement.
If someone cannot pay their share, discuss it before the payment date. Do not assume another person has agreed to cover it.
checklist: Try the example calculation with your own notes.

questions.prompt: Three people split £60 equally. What is each share?
questions.explanation: £60 divided by three is £20.

questions.prompt: What should the housemates agree before buying?
options: Only the colour of the receipt
Nothing until afterwards
The cost and each person’s share
questions.explanation: Agreeing the cost and shares first makes expectations clear.

questions.prompt: A person expects to miss the agreed payment date. What helps?
options: Tell the others early and discuss it
Say nothing
Assume someone else will pay
questions.explanation: An early conversation gives everyone time to discuss the situation.

lessons.title: Adjust for an unexpected cost
lessons.description: Practise changing a plan when something comes up.
reading_cards: Practice example: Taylor planned £40 of optional spending. A £15 replacement charger is needed. Using £15 from that amount leaves £25 for the original plans.
A spending plan can change. Write down the new cost and check which planned spending can wait rather than counting the same money twice.
If the example budget does not balance, pause and revise it. Completing this lesson does not mean you need to follow these particular amounts.
checklist: Try the example calculation with your own notes.

questions.prompt: Taylor starts with £40 and uses £15 for a charger. What remains?
questions.explanation: £40 minus £15 leaves £25.

questions.prompt: What should change when the new cost is added?
options: Nothing
Count the £15 twice
Update the amount left for other spending
questions.explanation: The same £15 cannot also be spent on the original plans.

questions.prompt: Which describes a useful practice budget?
options: A plan you can update
A promise never to change anything
A list that ignores new costs
questions.explanation: A plan is useful when you can revise it as circumstances change.

title: Managing money for the first time
description: Understand what comes in, what goes out and how to take the next step.

lessons.title: Make a simple money map
lessons.description: Start with information, not a perfect budget.
reading_cards: You do not need to understand everything today. Start with income, accounts you can access, regular bills and the next due dates. Use statements or official account information rather than guessing.
If someone else used to handle money, list what is unknown as well as what you know. An unfamiliar payment is something to investigate, not automatically something to cancel.

If this follows a death or another major change, ask the relevant bank or provider what access and documents are needed. This lesson is about your own day-to-day money; it does not establish authority to use someone else’s account.
checklist: List your income sources and next expected dates.
Find a recent statement for accounts you are authorised to access.
Write down three unknowns to ask a bank or provider about.

questions.prompt: You have a statement but do not recognise a £42 payment. What is a useful first action?
options: Check its reference and ask the bank or provider what it is
Cancel every regular payment
Assume it must be fraud without checking
questions.explanation: Identify the payment and any contractual obligation before deciding what to change.

questions.prompt: Which information helps build an initial money map?
options: A friend’s monthly spending
Income dates, bill dates and amounts
Only the account balance today
questions.explanation: Timing and commitments matter as well as the current balance.

questions.prompt: You know the login for an account in someone else’s name. Does that establish authority to use it?
options: Yes: knowing the password is enough
Yes: if you only make small payments
No: ask the bank about the appropriate process
questions.explanation: Knowing login details is not the same as being authorised to manage an account.

lessons.title: Read the payments on your statement
lessons.description: Understand Direct Debits and standing orders.
reading_cards: A Direct Debit lets a company collect an agreed payment from your bank account. A standing order is an instruction you set up to send a fixed amount regularly. A recurring card payment uses your card details.
If a Direct Debit has been collected in error, ask your bank about the Direct Debit Guarantee. A refund for a payment error does not erase a legitimate underlying debt.
Cancelling a payment instruction does not necessarily cancel the contract or what you owe. Check the agreement and contact the provider about ending or changing a service.
checklist: Identify one Direct Debit, standing order or card subscription on your statement.
Check the next amount and date with the provider if unclear.
Before cancelling, check the agreement and any remaining amount owed.

questions.prompt: You tell your bank to send £50 to your savings account every month. What is that?
options: A payslip deduction
A standing order
A Direct Debit collected by a company
questions.explanation: A standing order is a regular fixed payment you instruct your bank to send.

questions.prompt: You cancel the Direct Debit for a contract that still has six months left. What follows?
options: The contract automatically disappears
The provider must refund all past payments
You may still owe payments under the contract
questions.explanation: Stopping the bank instruction is different from ending the agreement.

questions.prompt: A company takes a Direct Debit twice by mistake. Who can you ask about the Guarantee?
options: Your bank
Only your employer
An unrelated social-media account
questions.explanation: Your bank can help with a Direct Debit error. Any valid underlying bill still needs resolving.

lessons.title: Plan what you can actually spend
lessons.description: Use a realistic monthly picture.
reading_cards: Alex receives £1,600 a month. Regular commitments are £1,050 and estimated food and travel are £350. That leaves £200 before any other costs, savings or debt payments.
Include costs that do not arrive every month. An expected £180 annual expense would need £15 a month set aside over a full year if starting from zero.
A budget is a working plan. Review real spending, update estimates and look for support if essentials exceed income. A shortfall is information, not a personal failure.
checklist: Use recent statements to estimate regular and variable costs.
Add a monthly allowance for known annual costs.
Set a short weekly check-in to compare your plan with reality.

questions.prompt: Alex has £1,600 income, £1,050 commitments and £350 food and travel. What remains?
questions.explanation: £1,600 − £1,050 − £350 = £200. Other costs may still need covering.

questions.prompt: You need £180 for an annual expense in 12 months, starting from zero. What is the monthly amount?
questions.explanation: £180 ÷ 12 = £15. A shorter timeframe would require a different amount.

questions.prompt: Your essential spending is higher than your income. What does the plan tell you?
options: The gap will disappear if you stop tracking it
There is a gap to address with support or changes
You have failed the task
questions.explanation: The plan makes a problem visible so you can consider realistic options and support.

lessons.title: Make the next call easier
lessons.description: Get help without giving away control.
reading_cards: Prepare a short list before contacting a bank or provider: what you want to understand, the account reference and the relevant dates. Keep a note of agreed next steps.
Use contact details from a trusted statement, card or official website. Never share a PIN or a one-time security code with someone who has unexpectedly contacted you.
You can ask a provider about accessible communication, extra time or support from a trusted person. Ask about their formal arrangements instead of sharing account passwords.
checklist: Choose one unanswered question and write it down.
Find the provider’s contact details independently.
Record the date, next step and any reference after the conversation.

questions.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be your bank and asks for a one-time code. What is safer?
options: End the call and contact the bank through a trusted route
Read out the code to prove who you are
Send the code by text instead
questions.explanation: Do not give an unexpected caller a security code. Verify independently.

questions.prompt: You want a trusted relative to help with calls. What should you ask the provider?
options: Whether they can remove all account security
What authorised support arrangements they offer
How to share your password with everyone
questions.explanation: Formal support can help you get assistance while keeping access appropriate.

questions.prompt: After agreeing a payment change, what is useful to keep?
options: Only the person’s first name
No record because it was discussed verbally
The date, agreed terms and reference
questions.explanation: A clear record helps you follow up and check whether the agreed change happened.

lessons.title: Stop, check and protect your money
lessons.description: Practise spotting suspicious calls, messages and investment offers.
reading_cards: A caller says they are from your bank and tells you to move money to a “safe account”. Stop. Do not make the transfer. End the call and contact your bank using a number on your card or statement, or its official app.

A familiar number on the screen does not prove who is calling. If you are checking a suspicious landline call, use a different phone if possible so the caller cannot keep the same line open. Never give an unexpected caller your PIN, password or one-time security code.

Someone offering to “fix” your computer or help with an investment may ask you to install software or share your screen. Do not give an unexpected caller remote control of a device. They could see information or operate your bank account.

Be cautious about guaranteed high returns, urgency or instructions to keep an offer secret. For financial services, check the FCA Firm Checker independently and use the contact details it lists. A genuine firm’s name can be copied; authorisation is not a guarantee that an investment is suitable or cannot lose money.

If you have sent money or shared details, contact your bank promptly through a trusted route. If a device may be under someone else’s control, use another trusted device or phone. Keep messages and payment details. Scams can happen to anyone: you deserve help, not blame.
checklist: Keep a trusted bank contact number somewhere you can find it without opening a message link.
Agree with yourself that an unexpected request for money or security codes can wait while you check.
If you have already acted, contact your bank promptly and keep relevant messages and transaction details.

sources.title: FCA · Banking and online account scams

questions.prompt: A caller claiming to be your bank says to transfer your savings to a “safe account”. What should you do?
options: End the call and contact your bank using a trusted number
Transfer a small amount first to test the account
Follow the instructions because the caller knows your name
questions.explanation: Do not move money on an unexpected caller’s instructions. Verify through a trusted route; names and caller numbers can be imitated.

questions.prompt: An unexpected investment caller asks you to install software so they can control your computer. What is the safer response?
options: Install it but hide your bank card
Decline, end the contact and independently check the firm
Allow access as long as they promise not to open your bank
questions.explanation: Remote access can let someone see private information or operate accounts. Do not grant it to an unexpected caller.

questions.prompt: You have already shared a code and notice an unfamiliar payment. What should you do next?
options: Wait to see if the money comes back
Pay someone who promises a guaranteed recovery
Contact your bank promptly through a trusted route and keep the evidence
questions.explanation: Act promptly using a trusted device or phone if yours may be compromised. You deserve support; do not let embarrassment delay asking for help.

lessons.title: Notice the small costs
lessons.description: Practise adding up everyday spending.
reading_cards: Practice example: Jo buys a £3 snack on five days. That adds up to £15. These are invented amounts, not a recommended spending limit.
Small purchases can be easy to forget. Writing them down can help explain where your money went.
You decide which purchases matter to you. A spending record is information, not a reason to feel guilty.

questions.prompt: What is £3 spent on five days?
questions.explanation: £3 multiplied by five is £15.

questions.prompt: What could help Jo remember small purchases?
options: Write them down
Ignore them
Guess at the end of the year
questions.explanation: A short record makes spending easier to see.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of keeping a spending record?
options: To blame yourself
To stop every enjoyable purchase
To understand your choices
questions.explanation: A record helps you make choices that fit your situation.

checklist: Try the example on paper at your own pace.

lessons.title: Do a five-minute money check
lessons.description: Build a simple habit for reviewing your plan.
reading_cards: Practice example: Lee has £100 available and a known £40 payment due before more money arrives. Reserving that payment leaves £60 for other costs.
A short check can include your available balance, payments still to come and any spending you have not yet recorded. Avoid counting the same money twice.
If a figure does not look right, check the details before changing your plan. You can make notes and ask someone you trust to help you understand them.

questions.prompt: Lee has £100 and reserves £40. What remains?
questions.explanation: £100 minus £40 leaves £60.

questions.prompt: What should a weekly check include?
options: Only yesterday’s balance
Only money already spent
Payments still to come
questions.explanation: Upcoming payments can reduce what is available to spend.

questions.prompt: A figure seems unfamiliar. What is a useful first step?
options: Check its details
Assume it must be correct
Forget about it
questions.explanation: Checking the details helps you understand what the figure represents.

checklist: Try the example on paper at your own pace.

title: Struggling to keep up with bills
description: Find a manageable next step. No streaks, deadlines or pressure to finish.

lessons.title: Work out what needs attention first
lessons.description: Start with consequences, not the loudest reminder.
reading_cards: If there is not enough money for everything, begin with essential living costs and bills whose non-payment could have serious consequences. Rent arrears, for example, can threaten your home; a louder credit-card reminder does not automatically make that bill more urgent.

Priority debt categories and available procedures differ across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Use guidance for your nation and speak with a free debt adviser about your circumstances.
A court deadline, eviction notice or risk of losing an essential service needs prompt help. You do not need to finish this course first: the support link is always available.
checklist: List overdue bills and any notices or deadlines.
Flag anything affecting your home, essential services or court action.
Use the free advice link if you are unsure what needs attention first.

sources.title: StepChange · Priority bills by UK nation

questions.prompt: You have rent arrears and a strongly worded credit-card reminder. What should guide priorities?
options: The consequences of missing each payment and your circumstances
Which company sends the most messages
Which envelope looks most official
questions.explanation: Priority is about consequences, including risks to your home, not pressure from the loudest creditor.

questions.prompt: A court notice gives a deadline next week. What is a sensible next step?
options: Throw it away because it is stressful
Seek appropriate advice promptly and keep the notice
Wait until every lesson is finished
questions.explanation: A learning app should not delay help with an urgent deadline.

questions.prompt: You find an England-specific debt procedure but live in Scotland. What should you do?
options: Assume all UK debt procedures are identical
Apply without checking where it operates
Check Scottish guidance or ask an adviser
questions.explanation: Processes and options vary across UK nations; use guidance that fits your location.

lessons.title: Prepare a conversation with a provider
lessons.description: Explain the problem and ask about realistic options.
reading_cards: Before calling, note your income, essential costs and what is overdue. You can say: “I am struggling with this bill. Can we discuss support and an arrangement based on what I can afford?”

If you have £1,300 income and £1,280 essential costs in a practice budget, the remaining £20 must be considered alongside all other commitments. It is not automatically an offer you should make to one creditor.
Ask what options are available, how they affect your account and whether interest or charges can be considered. Do not promise an amount you cannot maintain; an adviser can help assess affordability.
checklist: Write a brief explanation of what has changed.
Have your income, essential spending and other debts available.
Ask for any agreed arrangement in writing and check the next review date.

questions.prompt: Your budget leaves £20 before other debts. A provider requests £80 a month. What is appropriate?
options: Assume £20 must all go to this provider
Explain the affordability gap and seek help with a realistic arrangement
Promise £80 even though you cannot maintain it
questions.explanation: An arrangement should reflect the full budget, including other obligations.

questions.prompt: Which opening explains the situation usefully?
options: I will pay any amount you suggest
I cannot call until I have solved everything
I am struggling to pay; can we discuss support and what is affordable?
questions.explanation: You can ask for help before you have a complete solution.

questions.prompt: A new payment plan is proposed. What should you clarify?
options: Amounts, dates, charges and how the account will be treated
Only whether the call was short
Nothing once the provider says yes
questions.explanation: Understand the terms and consequences before relying on an arrangement.

lessons.title: Pause before borrowing to cover a gap
lessons.description: Compare the full commitment, not just today’s payment.
reading_cards: Borrowing can move a bill into the future without fixing a regular shortfall. Before taking new credit to cover existing debts, consider free debt advice and the full repayment commitment.
In a simplified comparison, option A requires £25 for six months: £150 total. Option B requires £18 for ten months: £180 total. A smaller monthly payment can still cost more overall.
Buy now, pay later is still a payment commitment. Check due dates, late-payment consequences and how it fits alongside rent, food and existing bills. Avoid pressure to decide immediately.
checklist: Write down the total repayment, dates and charges for any offer.
Check whether the gap is one-off or repeats every month.
Get free advice before taking new borrowing to repay existing debts.

questions.prompt: Which simplified option costs less overall: £25 for six months or £18 for ten?
options: £18 for ten months: £180
Both cost the same
£25 for six months: £150
questions.explanation: Multiply every instalment by the number of payments. Include fees when comparing real offers.

questions.prompt: Your income falls short of essentials every month. What does a new loan change?
options: It adds a repayment; it does not by itself solve the ongoing gap
It creates permanent extra income
It removes all future bills
questions.explanation: Repeated shortfalls need a wider plan and support, not just moving costs forward.

questions.prompt: A checkout offers four later payments. What should you treat them as?
options: Payments you can ignore after receiving the item
Future commitments in your budget
A discount that removes the cost
questions.explanation: Later payments still need funding and can have consequences if missed.

lessons.title: Find support without having everything ready
lessons.description: Take one manageable next step.
reading_cards: Free, confidential debt advice is available. MoneyHelper’s locator lets you find online, telephone or face-to-face support. An adviser can help you understand options and possible entitlements.
Bring what you have: recent bills, income information and letters are useful, but do not let an incomplete folder stop you seeking help. Explain any urgent deadlines first.

Support schemes and debt options depend on circumstances and where you live. Do not assume a solution mentioned online is available or suitable for everyone; ask an adviser to explain the consequences.
checklist: Open the advice locator and choose a contact method that suits you.
Gather the bills and income details you already have.
Write any urgent deadline at the top of your notes.

sources.title: StepChange · Priority bills by UK nation

questions.prompt: You are missing some statements but have an urgent bill problem. Should you wait?
options: No: seek help and explain which information is missing
Yes: advisers only help with perfect records
Yes: wait until all deadlines have passed
questions.explanation: Start with the information you have, especially when there is an urgent issue.

questions.prompt: What can a free debt adviser help you explore?
options: A requirement to take a new loan
Options and possible support suited to your circumstances
A guaranteed outcome for every person
questions.explanation: Advice helps assess your situation; it does not mean one solution fits everyone.

questions.prompt: A friend says one debt solution will solve everyone’s problems. What should you do?
options: Choose it because it helped your friend
Assume it works identically across the UK
Ask an adviser about eligibility, alternatives and consequences
questions.explanation: A suitable option depends on your circumstances and the relevant UK nation.

title: Starting your first job
description: Understand your payslip, bridge your first payday and build a useful routine.

lessons.title: Read your first payslip
lessons.description: Know the difference between gross and take-home pay.
reading_cards: Gross pay is earnings before deductions; net pay is what remains after them. In a fictional payslip, £2,000 gross minus £300 total deductions gives £1,700 net. These figures illustrate subtraction, not UK tax rates.
A payslip shows earnings and relevant deductions, such as Income Tax and National Insurance. Check the pay period, hours where relevant and the amount that reaches your bank.
If something does not match your agreed pay or hours, ask payroll to explain it. Keep payslips so you can check changes and provide evidence of earnings when needed.
checklist: Find gross pay, deductions and net pay on your own payslip.
Compare the period and hours with your records.
Ask payroll about any unexplained difference.

questions.prompt: A fictional payslip shows £2,000 gross and £300 total deductions. What is net pay?
questions.explanation: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions: £2,000 − £300 = £1,700.

questions.prompt: Which amount normally forms the starting point for your spending plan?
options: The employer’s total staffing cost
Take-home pay after deductions
Gross pay before deductions
questions.explanation: Use money actually available to you, then account for any other income or commitments.

questions.prompt: Your paid hours do not match your records. What helps resolve it?
options: Assume the bank can change your payslip
Ignore every future payslip
Compare the pay period and raise the difference with payroll
questions.explanation: Check the period first, then ask payroll to investigate with your records.

lessons.title: Bridge the gap to payday
lessons.description: Plan dates as well as amounts.
reading_cards: Starting work does not always mean being paid immediately. Ask about the payroll cut-off, first payment date and whether the first pay covers a full or partial period.
Riley has £240 before payday. Known travel is £60, food is £80 and a phone bill is £20, leaving £80 for other needs. These are practice figures; include your own essentials before making plans.
Once pay becomes regular, map bills against pay dates. If the timing does not fit, ask providers whether a due-date change is possible; confirm it before relying on it.
checklist: Confirm your first payday and the period it covers.
List essential costs between now and that date.
Check bill dates and ask about changes if the timing is difficult.

questions.prompt: Riley has £240, with £60 travel, £80 food and £20 phone due. What remains?
questions.explanation: £240 − £60 − £80 − £20 = £80, before any unlisted costs.

questions.prompt: You start halfway through a payroll period. What should you check?
options: Only the annual salary
Whether every employer pays on the same day
The first pay date, cut-off and period covered
questions.explanation: The first payment may cover a partial period or arrive later than expected.

questions.prompt: A bill is due before payday. What is a useful step?
options: Ask the provider about timing options and confirm any change
Move the date in your own calendar and assume it is agreed
Ignore the bill because you now have a job
questions.explanation: A reminder change does not change a contractual due date; speak with the provider.

lessons.title: Make sense of deductions
lessons.description: Know what to check and where to ask.
reading_cards: PAYE is the system employers use to collect Income Tax from pay. National Insurance is a separate deduction. Your tax code helps your employer work out tax; it is not itself a percentage rate.
If tax looks unexpected, check the employment details and tax code through HMRC’s official service and ask payroll about the calculation. A first payslip alone does not prove there is an error.

Student loan deductions depend on your loan plan and earnings rules. Thresholds and tax treatment can change, and Income Tax differs in Scotland. Use current official guidance rather than treating these fictional examples as a personal calculation.
checklist: Locate your tax code and deduction labels.
Check your employment information through HMRC if something looks wrong.
Ask payroll what each unfamiliar deduction relates to.

sources.title: GOV.UK · Check the tax on your payslip

questions.prompt: Your payslip has both Income Tax and National Insurance. Are they the same deduction?
options: Yes: one must always be a duplicate
Yes: the labels are interchangeable
No: they are separate
questions.explanation: They are distinct deductions. Seeing both does not itself mean tax was taken twice.

questions.prompt: Your tax code looks unfamiliar. What should you do?
options: Check HMRC’s official service and ask payroll if needed
Use a random online code for everyone
Assume the code is your tax percentage
questions.explanation: A tax code helps determine how pay is taxed; check the details rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: A colleague has a different student loan deduction. What matters?
options: Your deduction must be wrong
Their plan and earnings rules may differ from yours
Everyone must pay the identical amount
questions.explanation: Different plans and pay levels can produce different deductions. Check your own details.

lessons.title: Understand your pension and build a buffer
lessons.description: Balance future saving with money you can access.
reading_cards: A workplace pension is for retirement; it is different from an accessible emergency fund. Eligible workers are automatically enrolled and employers contribute under the applicable rules. Check the enrolment letter for your scheme.

Your pension contribution may reduce take-home pay, while employer contributions add to the pension. If you are considering leaving, understand what contributions or benefits you would lose and ask for guidance first.

For short-term surprises, choose an affordable amount for accessible savings only after considering essentials and your circumstances. A manageable plan can change over time; there is no single amount everyone must save.
checklist: Read your pension enrolment letter and contribution details.
Check how the contribution appears on your payslip.
Consider an affordable accessible buffer for short-term costs.

questions.prompt: You may need money for an unexpected expense next month. Which distinction matters?
options: A pension is retirement saving, not an everyday emergency pot
A pension is identical to a current account
All savings can always be withdrawn immediately
questions.explanation: Access rules differ. Retirement savings should not be treated as readily available spending money.

questions.prompt: You are thinking about leaving your workplace pension. What should you understand first?
options: Nothing: leaving never changes any benefits
The effect on your contributions and employer contributions
Only the colour of the scheme’s website
questions.explanation: Review the scheme and get guidance on consequences rather than deciding from one payslip line.

questions.prompt: You cannot afford a suggested savings target after essentials. What is reasonable?
options: Borrow solely to hit the target
Treat the suggested amount as compulsory
Choose a manageable plan or seek support, then review it
questions.explanation: Saving should fit your circumstances; an arbitrary target should not replace essentials.
